research-methods: Psychologists test hypotheses with operationally defined variables. Only an experiment, with a manipulated independent variable and random assignment, supports a cause-and-effect conclusion; correlational studies, case studies, naturalistic observation and surveys describe and predict. Control groups, placebos and blinding control confounding variables and expectations, and peer review, replication and meta-analysis decide which findings hold up.
research-sampling: A sample stands in for a population. Random sampling makes a representative sample likely, while convenience and self-selected samples are biased however large they are. Random sampling supports generalizing to the population; random assignment supports a causal claim. Whether results generalize to a group depends on how much the participants resemble that group in age, culture and setting.
stats-correlation: A correlation describes how two variables are related. On a scatterplot, points rising to the right show a positive correlation and points falling to the right a negative one; the correlation coefficient r gives the direction by its sign and the strength by its size, from 0 to 1. A correlation allows prediction but never shows cause: a third variable or the reverse direction may explain it, and some correlations people believe in are illusory.
heredity-environment: Behavior and mental processes come from heredity and environment working together. Twin, family and adoption studies estimate heritability, the share of variation in a trait within a group that is linked to genetic differences; it does not describe individuals or explain differences between groups. The evolutionary perspective explains shared human traits by natural selection, and its misuse in eugenics shows why claims about heredity must be read carefully.
nervous-system: The nervous system is made of neurons organized into two parts. The central nervous system, the brain and spinal cord, takes in information and decides. The peripheral nervous system links it to the body: its somatic division moves skeletal muscles on purpose, and its autonomic division runs the organs automatically, with the sympathetic division arousing the body for action and the parasympathetic division calming it again.
neural-firing: A neuron collects messages on its dendrites, and if its charge passes threshold it fires an all-or-none action potential down its axon, sped by myelin. At the terminals it releases neurotransmitters that cross the synapse, bind to receptors and excite or inhibit the next neuron, until reuptake ends the message. Hormones carry slower messages in the blood. Drugs act as agonists, antagonists or reuptake inhibitors, and repeated use brings tolerance and withdrawal.
research-ethics: Psychologists follow ethical guidelines that protect participants. A review board approves the plan; people give informed consent (minors give assent with a parent’s consent), may withdraw at any time, have their data kept confidential and are protected from harm. Deception is allowed only when necessary and low in risk, and it is always followed by debriefing. Animal research is reviewed for humane care. On the exam, name a safeguard the study describes and say how the researchers applied it.
brain: The brainstem keeps you alive and alert, the cerebellum smooths movement, and the limbic structures handle relay, drives, memory and fear. The cortex has four lobes, each with its own jobs, including the motor and somatosensory strips and the two language areas. Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, and the corpus callosum links them. We know this from damage cases, lesions, EEG and fMRI, and the brain can rewire through neuroplasticity.
sleep: Consciousness shifts across a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm. Each night the brain cycles about every 90 minutes through N1, N2 and deep N3, then REM, with N3 early and longer REM periods toward morning. Sleep restores the body and helps consolidate memories; activation-synthesis and consolidation theories explain dreams. When the cycle fails, the result can be insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnea, sleepwalking or REM sleep behavior disorder.
sensation: Sensation is detecting energy and transducing it into neural signals. Thresholds, Weber's law and signal detection describe what we notice, and adaptation and interaction change it. Rods and cones see; trichromatic and opponent-process theories explain color. Hair cells in the cochlea hear; place, frequency and volley theories explain pitch, and hearing loss is conduction or sensorineural. Smell, taste, touch, pain, balance and body position complete the senses.
perception: Perception turns sensations into meaning. It is built bottom-up from features and top-down from knowledge and expectations, filtered by limited attention, organized by Gestalt principles, given depth by binocular and monocular cues, and kept stable by perceptual constancy.
thinking: Thinking runs on concepts and prototypes, and schemas grow by assimilation and accommodation. Algorithms are slow and sure; heuristics are fast and usually right but produce predictable errors. Mental set and functional fixedness block solutions, framing and priming tilt choices, and executive functions and divergent thinking support good problem-solving.
memory-intro: Memory is encoding, storage and retrieval. Explicit memory (episodic and semantic) can be stated; implicit memory (procedural) shows in what we do; prospective memory is remembering to act. Information moves from sensory to short-term to long-term memory, working memory is the active workspace, deeper processing gives stronger memories, and long-term potentiation strengthens the synapses involved.
encoding-memories: Encoding improves when information is organized (mnemonics, the method of loci, chunking, hierarchies) and when study is spread out (distributed practice and the spacing effect) instead of crammed (massed practice). In a list, the first items (primacy) and last items (recency) are remembered best, giving the U-shaped serial position curve.
storing-memories: Repeating information (maintenance rehearsal) holds it briefly; linking it to meaning (elaborative rehearsal) stores it. New memories are consolidated over time with help from the hippocampus and sleep. Retrograde amnesia loses the past, anterograde amnesia blocks new memories, Alzheimer's disease gradually destroys memory, infantile amnesia is normal, and superior autobiographical memory is a rare extreme.
retrieving-memories: Retrieval depends on cues. Recognition is usually easier than recall because the options are cues. Matching the place, body state or mood of learning helps retrieval. Practicing retrieval (the testing effect) strengthens memory more than rereading, and good metacognition means checking what you know by testing yourself instead of trusting familiarity.
forgetting: We forget quickly at first and then more slowly (the forgetting curve). Forgetting comes from encoding failure, interference (proactive and retroactive) and retrieval failure; repression is the psychodynamic account, with weak evidence. Because memory is reconstructed, misleading information, forgotten sources and imagination can produce confident false memories.
stats-descriptive: Descriptive statistics summarize a set of numbers. The mean, median and mode describe the center; the range and standard deviation describe the spread. Outliers pull the mean toward them, so in a skewed distribution the median is the better summary of a typical value. A frequency distribution or histogram shows the shape: symmetric, skewed toward a tail, or bimodal with two peaks.
stats-normal: In a normal distribution, scores form a symmetric bell curve around the mean. By the 68-95-99.7 rule, about 68% of scores lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. A z score gives a score’s distance from the mean in standard deviations, which lets you compare scores from different tests, and a percentile rank gives the percent of scores below it.
stats-significance: Inferential statistics let researchers judge whether a sample’s result reflects the population. A statistically significant difference ( p < .05 ) is unlikely to be due to chance alone; a difference that is not significant could plausibly be chance. Significance does not measure size: effect size tells how big a difference is, and with very large samples even tiny effects can be significant.
intelligence: Intelligence tests measure a general ability (g) that shows up across many tasks, though some theories stress separate abilities. Modern scores are standardized on a normal curve (mean 100, SD 15) and must be reliable and valid. Scores are shaped by context (stereotype threat and lift, the Flynn effect), group gaps are not explained by within-group heritability, tests have a history of misuse, and beliefs about ability (growth and fixed mindsets) affect effort.
development-methods: Developmental psychology asks how people change and stay the same across life, framed by nature and nurture, continuity and discontinuity, and stability and change. Cross-sectional studies compare age groups at once and risk cohort effects; longitudinal studies follow the same people and risk dropout and long timelines. Neither assigns age, so neither alone shows cause.
physical-development: Physical development runs from before birth to old age. Teratogens can harm the developing baby. Newborns have reflexes, and motor milestones follow maturation in a similar order with varied timing. Critical and sensitive periods show that timing matters. Puberty brings sex characteristics, menarche and spermarche, while the brain keeps maturing into the 20s. Adulthood brings gradual sensory and motor decline and menopause.
gender-orientation: Sex refers to biology; gender to identity and to the roles a culture expects. Gender identity is a person’s inner sense of their gender, and gender typing is how children learn their culture’s gender roles. Sexual orientation is a separate, lasting pattern of attraction, shaped by many factors and not by parenting. Most average differences between girls and boys are small.
cognitive-development: Piaget described four stages of thinking, from object permanence in infancy, through the egocentrism and failed conservation of the preschool years, to logical and then abstract thought; research supports his order more than his ages. Vygotsky added that learning moves forward with scaffolding in the zone of proximal development. In adulthood, crystallized intelligence holds while fluid intelligence slowly declines, and dementia is a disease, not normal aging.
language-development: Language has layers, from phonemes to morphemes to words, organized by grammar: semantics for meaning and syntax for order. It is generative, so rules make endless new sentences. Children move from cooing to babbling, single words and telegraphic speech, tuning in to their home language’s sounds in the first year and overgeneralizing grammar rules as they learn them.
social-emotional-development: Social and emotional development happens inside nested systems, from family to culture. Attachment grows from contact comfort and responsive care and is classified as secure, avoidant, anxious or disorganized. Parenting styles and temperament shape each other. Erikson’s eight psychosocial stages, identity statuses, the imaginary audience and personal fable, emerging adulthood and the social clock mark later development, and adverse childhood experiences raise average risk without deciding any one life.
classical-conditioning: Classical conditioning is learning by association. A neutral stimulus that comes just before an unconditioned stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers a conditioned response. Extinction weakens that response, spontaneous recovery shows the learning is still there, generalization spreads it and discrimination narrows it. Biology sets limits: some links, such as taste with illness, form after one pairing.
operant-conditioning: Operant conditioning changes voluntary behavior through its consequences. Reinforcement, positive or negative, increases a behavior; punishment, positive or negative, decreases it. Shaping builds new behaviors step by step, while instinctive drift, superstitious behavior and learned helplessness show its limits. Ratio schedules produce faster responding than interval schedules, and partial reinforcement makes behavior last longer than continuous reinforcement.
social-cognitive-learning: Not all learning needs direct reinforcement. In observational learning, people attend to and remember what models do and imitate them more when models are rewarded (vicarious reinforcement) and less when they are punished (vicarious punishment), even though the behavior is learned either way. Latent learning and cognitive maps show learning that stays hidden until it is useful, and insight learning is a sudden whole solution. Brain reward circuits are one biological part of how consequences strengthen behavior.
attribution: Attribution theory describes how people explain behavior, by disposition or by situation. Explaining others mostly by disposition is the fundamental attribution error; switching between situation for yourself and disposition for others is the actor-observer bias; crediting yourself for success and the situation for failure is the self-serving bias. Locus of control and explanatory style describe how people explain their own outcomes, and the mere exposure effect, self-fulfilling prophecies, social comparison and relative deprivation shape how we see others and ourselves.
attitudes: Attitudes combine feelings and beliefs about people and things. Stereotypes, cognitive load and implicit attitudes can feed prejudice, and the just-world phenomenon, in-group bias, out-group homogeneity and ethnocentrism keep it going. Confirmation bias and belief perseverance make attitudes resist change, while cognitive dissonance, the discomfort of acting against an attitude, can change them. The classic dissonance findings hold up in part; a large 2024 replication found attitude change but not every prediction.
social-situations: Situations shape behavior powerfully. People conform for information or acceptance and often obey authority; persuasion works by central or peripheral routes and by request techniques. Groups can polarize views, silence doubts (groupthink), improve easy performance (social facilitation), reduce effort (social loafing) and lower restraint (deindividuation). Helping depends on norms and on the situation: the bystander effect lowers each person's chance of helping, but in real public conflicts recorded on camera, someone usually helps. Classic studies are taught with their limits: Milgram's results partly replicate, and the Stanford prison study's methods are seriously flawed.
psychodynamic-humanistic: The psychodynamic view explains personality through unconscious processes and the defense mechanisms that protect us from anxiety (repression, denial, displacement, projection, rationalization, reaction formation, regression, sublimation), assessed with projective tests whose reliability and validity are often weak. The humanistic view stresses growth: when people receive unconditional positive regard, the self-actualizing tendency moves them toward their potential. Both views are influential but hard to test.
social-cognitive-trait: The social-cognitive view explains personality as reciprocal determinism among person factors, behavior and environment, with self-concept, self-esteem and self-efficacy as key person factors. Trait theories describe stable tendencies; factor analysis of trait ratings yields the Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism), measured with personality inventories. Traits are fairly stable across adulthood but still change, and situations shape how they show.
motivation: Motivation theories explain different behavior: instincts for fixed animal patterns, drive-reduction for body needs and homeostasis, incentives for outside pulls, arousal theory and the Yerkes-Dodson law for the best level of arousal, and self-determination theory for intrinsic motivation, which expected rewards can undermine (the overjustification effect). Motivational conflicts are approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, approach-avoidance and multiple approach-avoidance. Hunger involves ghrelin, leptin, the hypothalamus and external cues; the need to belong drives social behavior.
emotion: Emotion combines physiological arousal, a felt experience and expression. Theories differ in sequence: arousal first, then the feeling; arousal and feeling at the same time; or arousal plus a cognitive appraisal that labels it, with some fast reactions coming before appraisal. The facial feedback hypothesis has mixed evidence. Some emotions are recognized across cultures above chance, though better within one's own culture, and display rules shape expression. Broaden-and-build theory says positive emotions widen thinking and build resources.
health-psychology: Health psychology studies how stress and behavior affect physical health. Stress depends on how we appraise stressors: eustress motivates, distress harms. Daily hassles and adverse childhood experiences are linked to poorer health. Under threat, the sympathetic nervous system drives fight-flight-freeze, and people may also tend and befriend. With a long stressor, the general adaptation syndrome moves from alarm to resistance to exhaustion, when illness becomes more likely. Problem-focused coping changes the stressor; emotion-focused coping manages the feelings.
positive-psychology: Positive psychology scientifically studies what helps people thrive. Subjective well-being is a person's own judgment of life satisfaction and feelings. Resilience, bouncing back after adversity, is common; posttraumatic growth is positive change after a struggle with trauma. Gratitude practices and using signature strengths show small benefits. Character strengths are grouped into six virtues: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance and transcendence.
explaining-disorders: A psychological disorder is a pattern of thinking, feeling or behaving that is unusual for its cultural setting and causes distress or dysfunction. Clinicians classify disorders with the DSM-5-TR or the ICD. Each psychological perspective explains disorders in its own way, and the biopsychosocial and diathesis-stress models combine causes: a vulnerability plus enough stress.
disorders: The DSM-5-TR groups disorders by their core features. Depressive and bipolar disorders differ by whether mania or hypomania occurs. Schizophrenia involves positive and negative symptoms and is not dissociative identity disorder. Anxiety disorders center on fear and worry; OCD, PTSD, the dissociative disorders, the eating disorders and the three clusters of personality disorders each have their own categories. Learn the core feature and the time rule for each.
treatment: Each approach to therapy targets a different cause: psychodynamic therapy seeks insight into unconscious conflicts, humanistic therapy offers acceptance, behavioral therapy changes learned responses, cognitive therapy changes thoughts, and CBT combines the two. Biomedical treatments change brain chemistry or activity. Good care is evidence-based, built on a strong therapeutic alliance and cultural humility, and guided by ethics such as informed consent and confidentiality.
